# Issues — archive

**Closed items, moved out of `ISSUES.md` so the register stays the list of what
is live.** Nothing here is open. Ids are never reused and never renumbered, so a
`FJS-###` named anywhere in the repo resolves either there or here.

**When a row moves.** `ISSUES.md` § Closed keeps the most recent closures and is
trimmed when it passes ~40 rows, by `fli register:archive`. A count rule rather than an age rule, because
closures arrive in bursts — 37 of these were closed on one day, and a date rule
alone lets one busy day bury a month. Everything older comes here, copied
verbatim: a row is never rewritten or summarized on the way in.

**Why keep them at all.** The same reason § Closed exists: a stale document, an
old handoff, or a comment in code can name an id and imply it is still broken.
This is how that gets refuted with the evidence attached — what the defect was,
what changed, and how it was proven. It is also the record of what building each
package actually cost, which no single changelog carries.

Read it when tracing something specific, never cold. `ISSUES.md` is the file
that answers *what is wrong right now*.

Measured 2026-10-04: 208 invoices on `SUB-3001` and 218 versions. Three effects follow. (1) The pages ask for 50 rows newest-first, so `subDetail.changePlan` waits for an invoice count that cannot rise (this is `FJS-1376`'s cause), and `verify:account`'s *and their invoices* never sees `INV-3001`. (2) `planDetail.newWindowEmpty` never sees version 1, the one `SUB-3001` holds. (3) The unpaid invoices lapse `SUB-3001` to `pastDue` through dunning, which reddens `subDetail.stopRenewing`. `db:seed` upserts and deletes nothing, so it heals none of this. `verify:account` also throws before its cleanup runs, which leaves `SUB-ACC*`/`SUB-OTH*`/`INV-A*`/`INV-Q*` behind on every run. | <a id="fjs-1061"></a>FJS-1061 | cli — **A tutor lesson ADOPTS whatever is already answering on its port, so a person with their own app on 8000 runs the whole lesson against it and is told the framework is broken.** Found 2026-09-09. `ensureApi` and `ensureWeb` ask health FIRST and use anything that answers ([_module.md](packages/cli/commands/tutor/_module.md)), which the comment beside them states as deliberate — *which is also what a person with the app open in another terminal wants*. It cannot tell that app from a DIFFERENT one: `tutor:ui` and `tutor:app` default to `--api-port 8000 --web-port 8100`, the dev slot for project 0, which is exactly where the app somebody scaffolded an hour ago is listening. **Every symptom points at the lesson.** The register succeeded (a real API answered), the page loaded (a real web server answered), and sign-in failed with *no token in this origin's storage* against a login form belonging to another product entirely — the diagnosis printed was `the sign-in form is the app's own /login/ page`, which is advice that cannot be taken. Three runs and about an hour to find, and the same three lines are what a first-time user sees. **`FJS-740`'s shape one layer up**, and the drives table's own rule — *a port that answers is not evidence the right process is on it*. **The fix is one question the lesson can actually ask**: the tutor knows the app it scaffolded, so a health answer has to be checked against it — the app NAME off `/api/health` (junction already answers it) or a build stamp — before it is adopted, and refused by name otherwise. `startServer` already refuses a busy port; it is the adopt path that has no identity check. Not the ports: moving the default to the test tier hides it for the lesson and leaves the mechanism | 2026-10-22 | Cause: ensureApi/ensureWeb adopted any process whose port answered, so a different app on the default dev slot (8000/8100) ran the whole lesson. Fix: core/probe.js apiIsApp/pageIsApp compare /api/health's `app` and the page <title> with the scaffolded app name; a mismatch is a `foreign` failure naming the app found and the --api-port/--web-port way out, refused rather than adopted (startServer untouched). `must` shows the probe's own `likely`. Proved by test/probe.test.js apiIsApp/pageIsApp; cli suite green bar FJS-3262. · [_module.md `ensureApi`/`ensureWeb`](packages/cli/commands/tutor/_module.md) · [ui.md](packages/cli/commands/tutor/ui.md) · [FJS-740](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-740) |

| <a id="fjs-1026"></a>FJS-1026 | sierra — **A navigation that FAILS is invisible to the code that asked for it: `goto` resolves the same whether it committed or was refused.** **Corrected 2026-09-13**: a route module that throws at import no longer rejects anything — `_navigate` catches it, reports it through `_reportError` (the dev overlay where one is installed, `console.error` otherwise) and returns, so `goto` resolves identically either way. The console half is answered; the caller half is not — `location` does not change, the page shows the form it was already showing, and nothing a caller holds says so. **Three things a person can be looking at, none of which distinguish this from the others**: the write succeeded and the redirect failed, the write failed and its error was swallowed, or the click never registered. It cost an hour to tell them apart, with a real create in the API log and a `service_result` frame captured on the socket, because the only remaining place to look was a body dump of the destination route. Of the two candidate fixes the first, reporting a failed import, has landed; what is owed is the second — `goto` answering whether it committed, so a create-then-redirect can say so | 2026-10-21 | Cause: `_navigate` returned undefined on every path, so `goto` resolved identically for a commit, a guard cancel, a failed route import, a stopped redirect loop and a navigation a newer one overtook. Fix: `_navigate` answers a boolean — `true` only after the commit and after-hooks, `false` on every refusal, a redirect passing its callee's answer through — and `goto` returns it (never rejects; the refusal is still reported where it happens). Proof: five tests in `packages/sierra/test/router-hardening.test.js` (§ FJS-1026) went red against the undefined return and pass; sierra suite 2408 green. Cost: 12 bytes on the spa bench, adopted. Drives need Chrome (FJS-3367) and were not run. · [router/index.js § goto, _navigate](packages/sierra/src/router/index.js) · [FJS-1025](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1025) |

| <a id="fjs-1423"></a>FJS-1423 | mesa — **`bind:value={pick[l.id]}` (a bind to a MEMBER of a `let`) compiles clean and writes the member in place, so nothing else that reads the `let` re-renders. Compiled: `$$runtime.bindInput($$el, 'value', () => ($$runtime.get($$sig_pick)[l().id]), ($$v) => { $$runtime.get($$sig_pick)[l().id] = $$v; })`, with no `set`, against `bind:value={one}` → `$$set_one`. Fix: the compiler owns this setter, so for a member target it can emit the write followed by `$$set_pick($$runtime.get($$sig_pick))`, which is the `obj = obj` the docs ask for. | <a id="fjs-268"></a>FJS-268 | repo — **A consuming app's `tsc` reported the framework's type errors, not its own — and all of them came from junction.** Every `@frontierjs` package points its `exports` at a `.ts` and none emits `.d.ts`, so tsc follows those imports and checks the framework as part of the app's program; `skipLibCheck` covers `.d.ts` only and there is no option for *check my files, not the ones they import*. **Measured rather than assumed, and the measurement moved the fix**: of the 61 diagnostics a freshly scaffolded app saw, 61 were junction's — auth, caravan, conduit, notifications and testing ship `.ts` too and were already clean. Junction carries no typecheck baseline now, which is 0. **What stays open is the structural half**, and it is a cost question rather than a correctness one: an app still compiles the whole framework on every `tsc` run and in its editor, and `fli typecheck` filters the output rather than preventing the work. Shipping `.d.ts` beside the source would stop it and give an editor types it does not have to compile — against it, two artefacts to keep in step, and a `.d.ts` that drifts from its `.ts` is worse than none. Nothing forces the decision now that the output is clean | 2026-10-19 | Correctness half fixed 2026-08-15 (junction's consumer surface type-clean, baseline 0). The structural half — an app's tsc and editor compiling the framework's .ts source — was ruled by FJS-D1028 (B): stay source-only, keep fli typecheck's output filter (typecheck.js suppresses diagnostics from files outside the package) as the answer, per-run compile cost accepted; revisit with a drift-checked .d.ts emit (A) only when typecheck time or editor lag is measured on a real app. Nothing left to fix, so no red test; confirmed by running the package typecheck, whose only non-package lines are suppressed. · [typecheck.js](packages/cli/core/typecheck.js) · [junction/tsconfig.json](packages/junction/tsconfig.json) |

| <a id="fjs-610"></a>FJS-610 | example — **A soft decline is never re-presented, so every invoice is charged exactly once and the distinction the code makes between soft and hard buys nothing.** `declineKind` separates *the money may be there tomorrow* from *this card will never work*, and the whole value of the first is that the clock keeps running and the charge is tried again. Nothing tries it again: `subscription-renew` dispatches `invoice-collect` once, and dunning moves STATES — `Invoice`'s two `@@commitment`s lapse at the grace and cancel at the deadline, `recoverIfClear` recovers when the ledger is clean — and dispatches nothing. So a soft-declined invoice sits `issued` until the deadline cancels the subscription, having been presented one time. **Caravan's retry ladder does not cover it and cannot**: a transport failure throws and retries, but a decline is a domain ANSWER returned as a value, which exits the ladder successfully. The fix is a re-presentment with a clock of its own, under `unique` for [`FJS-609`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-609)'s reason, with the cadence a decision rather than a default — a shop that re-presents daily for 21 days is a shop the card networks notice. Not a defect in anything built: every piece is correct on its own, and this is the half the design implies and nobody wrote. `verify:collect` asserts the soft decline leaves the subscription alone, which is true and is not the same as the money being asked for again | 2026-10-18 | Cause: a decline is a returned answer, so caravan's ladder never saw it and the one invoice-collect dispatch was the only presentment. Fix: on a soft payment.failed for an issued invoice, payments.service record dispatches invoice-collect again with delay RETRY_DAYS[failedCount-1] days and unique occurrenceKey('collect', invoiceId, attempt) (FJS-D907: RETRY_DAYS [1,3,5,7] in billing.ts, attempt counted from the invoice's failed Payments, stops at the ladder's end, a hard decline or a non-issued invoice). Proof: verify:collect retry.* (first queues one a day out, second climbs to 3 days, hard queues nothing, ladder ends) red before, green after. · [schema.lite `Invoice`](example/db/schema.lite) · [billing.ts `declineKind`](example/api/src/domain/billing/billing.ts) |

| <a id="fjs-d1204"></a>FJS-D1204 | toolbelt — **How does a template's sender form check a typed value: does mergeFields validate it, or does it hand Sierra's existing field rules a schema to grade?** | 2026-10-18 | Ruled [`FJS-D1204`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1204): **B** — `mergeFields` grows `schema(filter?)` → a JSON Schema object (`number` → `{ type: 'number' }`, `date` → `{ type: 'string', format: 'date' }`, `default` → `default`), and the form is `createResource`/`Form` over it, so `buildFieldRules`, `coerceToSchema` and `controlFor` (Invariant 4's owners of translation and control choice) grade and draw it. | <a id="fjs-d1098"></a>FJS-D1098 | junction — **What is the wire spelling and the envelope of a tree read — one structured $recursive directive graded at the Data boundary, a flat family, or no directive and a built-in read method?** | 2026-10-18 | Ruled [`FJS-D1098`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1098): **A** — one `$recursive` row in `DIRECTIVES` (`asIs`, OPAQUE schema, as `$orderBy`): the value is `{ direction, maxDepth, nested, via }`, travels as a structure (`$recursive[direction]=ancestors`, `FJS-D125`) and litestone grades the keys and refuses the unsupported combinations by name (`count`, `aggregate`, `limit` under `nested`). | <a id="fjs-1086"></a>FJS-1086 | example — **A browser drive running while anyone edits a watched file is RELOADED under its feet, and the failure reads as a bug on whatever screen it had reached.** Found 2026-09-12 chasing [FJS-1084](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1084): eight `[vite] (client) page reload packages/sierra/src/router/*.js` lines landed in the web server's log inside one run, because another session was editing the router, and each one full-reloaded the drive's page. Fix: verify.mjs records any main-frame Page.frameNavigated arriving while no goto() is in flight and, on a throw or at the end of a passing run, fails naming the reload. Measured: touching a sierra router file every 4s mid-run fails with 'the page was RELOADED under the drive'; the undisturbed control passes all 71 assertions. Other web/test drives share the hazard and are not guarded. · [verify.mjs](example/web/test/verify.mjs) · [FJS-1084](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-1084) |

| <a id="fjs-d1206"></a>FJS-D1206 | litestone — **What does a model with no @@gate and no policy, or a model-less custom method with no gate:, allow — deny below system, deny writes only, open but loud, or a parse error?** | 2026-10-17 | Ruled [`FJS-D1206`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1206): **A** — deny by default, reads included. A model with no gate and no policy refuses every operation below the system principal, and a written `@@gate("0.…")` is how a model says public, so no new word is needed. A model-less custom method with no `gate:` refuses below system, and `gate: 0` (the spelling `warnFloorRefusal` already prints, `packages/junction/src/core/litestone.ts:3342`) says open. This amends `FJS-D516`'s "an ungated model reads at 0". It is ZenStack (no `allow` means deny, [policy-handler.ts](https://github.com/zenstackhq/zenstack-v3/blob/dev/packages/plugins/policy/src/policy-handler.ts)), PocketBase (a `null` rule is superusers only), Payload (`defaultAccess` requires a logged-in user), Amplify Gen 2 ("deny-by-default"), Hasura (no permissions until added), Directus and Firestore production mode. · [IDEAS/pen-testing.md](IDEAS/pen-testing.md) |

| <a id="fjs-585"></a>FJS-585 | cli — **A Release records a configuration set that nothing applies, so `configurationHash` identifies the DECLARED configuration and not the one the process is running on.** `configurationSet(deployConf, target)` resolves `deploy.configuration` and `deploy.secrets`, hashes them into the Release id and writes the values and secret references into the journal — and no step ever puts them on the target. The container is started with `--env-file ${envFile}`, which is `.env.production` on the machine; `fli` READS that file (`01b-env-check` compares its keys against `.env.example`) and MOUNTS it, and writes it nowhere. So the two descriptions of one Release's configuration are independent, and a `configuration:` block edited in `frontier.config.js` changes the Release id, the generation and the recorded values while the running process is unchanged — a redeploy that mints a visibly different Release and alters nothing. Half of it is already known and stated: `fli deploy:revert` refuses to restore the pair once the generation has moved, saying it writes no `.env` on a target and therefore genuinely cannot. What is not stated is the other direction — that the hash is a fact about a file in the repository rather than about the deployment — and invariant 2 of `IDEAS/release-transitions.md` is written as though it were the latter (*serving state is the pair (Release, Generation)*). Found 2026-08-29 while wiring attached services ([`FJS-D158`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d158)), which is why that check grades `process.env` rather than the recorded set. **Half-addressed 2026-08-30**: the Release now says the hash covers a DECLARATION (`formatRelease` prints `(declared)`, `release:mint`'s table and `core/release.js`'s header say so), and `01b-env-check` grades the target against the declared KEYS — so the block asserts *this environment carries these* instead of being vacuous, and a declared block turns the check on by itself. What remains is the values half. Two honest ways out and they are different features: `fli` writes the env file from the configuration set (which makes the pair real and puts secret RESOLUTION on the critical path), or the Release records that its configuration is unmanaged and the hash covers only what it can see. | 2026-10-17 | Cause: a Release hashed and journaled `deploy.configuration` but no step put it on the target. Proved by deploy-helpers.test.js swapContainer tests (red before, green after), release-mint.test.js key refusals, and the cli suite (only FJS-3230 fails, unrelated). · [release-transitions.md](IDEAS/release-transitions.md) · [`FJS-D747`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d747) |

| <a id="fjs-503"></a>FJS-503 | litestone · junction — **`input:` validates a custom method's payload and types nothing, so the method body opens with a hand cast that can assert anything.** `{ method: 'recordTracking', input: 'TrackingUpdate' }` names a `type` in the seed and the payload really is checked against it — and then the body writes `const { trackingCode } = $.data as { trackingCode: string }`, under a comment in `example` defending the cast on the grounds that the validator already ran. The defense is true and TypeScript cannot see any of it: `as { trackingCode: number }` compiles identically, and the next line reads a field that is not there. **A generated surface that omits the one thing the declaration was for is the shape of `FJS-250`.** **Both halves already exist and nothing joins them.** `typegen.js` emits every seed `type` as a real interface (`export interface TrackingUpdate { trackingCode: string }`, line 123), and `ServiceTypes` beside it already proves the pattern — a generated registry, module-augmented, so `client.service('posts')` infers with no import and no type argument. The missing piece is one more registry: emit `SeedTypes { TrackingUpdate: TrackingUpdate, … }`, make `input:` `keyof SeedTypes` so a typo is a compile error rather than a boot throw, and have junction index `SeedTypes[T]` to type `$.data` inside that method. The service file does not change and the snapshot does not change. **Considered and rejected: importing the type instead** — `input: types.TrackingUpdate`. It makes a hand-written declaration depend on a generated file having been built, gives a JS app an import that does nothing, and duplicates a name that has to keep existing anyway because `surface.snapshot.md` records inputs by name and the validator resolves by name. Passing the schema OBJECT is worse still: the seed stops being the runtime owner and a stale artefact validates against last week's rules. **The rule that decides it, and it explains the three existing choices rather than contradicting them**: an early-bound handle where the thing pointed at is hand-written in the same language (caravan's `defineJob`), a name plus a registry where it is generated from another one (`input:`) or where the boundary cannot import (`registerControl`). What is given up is go-to-definition on a string, and the mitigation is the editor rather than the API — the vscode extension already jumps from `model:` into the seed, and jumping to the seed is the better destination than jumping to the artefact | 2026-10-17 | Cause: `input:` was a bare string, so nothing joined the validator to the body's type. Fix (FJS-D876 B): typegen emits `SeedTypes` beside the seed interfaces and, with `--augment junction`, augments junction's empty `SeedTypes`; `MethodDeclaration.input` is `keyof SeedTypes` once augmented (plain string before), and `defineMethod('TrackingUpdate', ctx => …)` types `ctx.data` as `SeedTypes[T]` while carrying the name `collectMethodInputs` reads, so the handle alone declares the input (an entry that disagrees is refused). Example's recordTracking no longer casts. Proof: client-types.test.ts tsc fixture (inference, two `@ts-expect-error`, typo refused; red under a stubbed `SeedData`), method-input.test.ts § defineMethod, litestone.test.ts SeedTypes case; junction suite 3105 pass, typecheck clean. · [typegen.js](packages/litestone/src/tools/typegen.js) · [junction litestone.ts `validateInput`](packages/junction/src/core/litestone.ts) · [example orders.service.ts](example/api/src/services/orders.service.ts) |

A session gone closes the app's socket 4001 (a raw route's 1001), a changed principal 1001, a throwing provider 1011; an unchanged answer keeps the old object for the cohort memo. | <a id="fjs-d1145"></a>FJS-D1145 | litestone — **How does allocating an @@extensible slot avoid a whole-tenant scan when the slot is not the slot index's leading column: a freed-slot record on the declaring table, the clear moved off the declaration, or one index per slot?** | 2026-10-17 | Ruled [`FJS-D1145`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1145): **A** — the allocator records each slot it hands out, per (model, tenant, scope), in a table Litestone owns, never on the app's declaring model, which would gain rows the app never wrote. A slot that is neither in that record nor in the `taken` set the allocator already reads has never held a value, so it needs no clear. A slot in the record clears, and takes the scan, exactly as today. A tenant's first fill of its pool (every Posthog declaration) costs nothing. Reuse pays one scan per reuse. The record is written by the one path that allocates, not by the delete, so a declaration deleted outside the client still leaves its slot recorded and clearing on reuse. A slot STATED on a raw insert skips the allocator, so it goes unrecorded unless it is still taken. Invariant 1 holds. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |

A row-scoped write with no `before` (cross-process, which stores ids; `select: false`; bulk `rows` mode) sends no removal, failing closed. Cost: one extra SELECT per tapped single-row update, and bulk `announce: 'rows'` reads N rows; a cross-process write can no longer revoke a row from a store live. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |
| <a id="fjs-d1201"></a>FJS-D1201 | junction — **Who ends an open socket whose session is revoked or whose principal changes after the upgrade — auth at each session-ending write, the transport re-verifying the socket's session, or both** | 2026-10-17 | Ruled [`FJS-D1201`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d1201): **B** — The transport re-verifies: the socket keeps its upgrade credential, and `IAuth.verifySession` is asked again on every incoming frame (HTTP's cost per request) and on an interval for a socket that only receives. | <a id="fjs-620"></a>FJS-620 | litestone — **Findings from the performance audit that are in no other register, so they depend on somebody reading a July document.** [`FJS-112`](ISSUES.md#fjs-112) exists and is about the METHOD — no owner, no gate, no committed baselines — and the still-open list it names in passing covers H8, H9, JSONL cold-load streaming, S3 streaming/multipart and a low-impact tail. Five medium findings are named in neither it nor either idea document: **M4** nested writes — the atomicity half is closed by [`FJS-638`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-638), which put nested writes inside the transaction machinery, and what stands is that they run one statement per child; **M5** variable-length `IN (?,?,…)` lists compile a distinct statement per value-count and churn the 500-entry LRU, **and there is no chunking guard for SQLite's bind-variable limit**, which is a correctness cliff rather than a slow one; **M11** (closed: `resolveAllRowCounts` counts each table once through `countRows`, `getTableStats` keeps the whole-file pricing for the one-table bytes limit; `test/transform-row-counts.test.ts`); **M12** the retention pass, whose first-line early exit and O(n²) `shift()` loop both landed but whose un-indexed `DELETE … WHERE createdAt < ?` still full-scans unless the app happened to index the column — the audit's fix was to auto-create it when a `database` block declares `retention`. **M7 was the fifth and is closed** ([`FJS-619`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-619)). Not one issue per finding, because the audit is the detail and duplicating it here is how the two disagree; this is the pointer that makes them open. **The 2026-10-09 performance audit re-confirmed M4 and M5, measured M5's cliff, and adds M6 here**: M5 (its R6) — 64 IN-list lengths compile 64 statements, the LRU churn that triggered [FJS-2309](ISSUES.md#fjs-2309)'s finalize; 40,000 values work (13.7 ms), 100,000 throw Bun's raw *expected 34464 values*, and the wasm engine's default limit is 32,766. **M5 closed 2026-10-10**: past four values a list binds as one JSON array through `inList` (query.js) — the caller's `in`/`notIn`/bare array/`hasNone`, every include and `_count` key list, the soft-delete cascade and restore, the edge lookups, FTS rowids, and a policy's list against a column. The audit's `SELECT value` was wrong on a TEXT column: a json_each value takes no affinity, so `name IN (1)` missed the text '1' a bound list matches; `CAST(value AS TEXT)` lets the column's own affinity convert it back, exact on TEXT, INTEGER and REAL, float precision included. It is wrong on a column with no affinity, so the trail's `Any` columns and expression operands (a json_each value, a json_extract path) take the value uncast, and a @from operand, a policy path, a caller with no field kinds and a value JSON cannot carry keep the bound list, as do composite keys. Proved by test/in-list.test.ts (a hand-written bound list as the oracle, column type by column type, both directions; 60 lengths are one statement; 100,000 values answer) and a browser-drive case (numbers asked of a String column, 40,000 values past the wasm limit). Per execution the two forms are even up to ~20 values and JSON is ~20% slower at 100–1,000 on an already-prepared statement. sierra test:safety 12/12; basecamp verify:screens 117/118 on the 7120 slot, and its one failure (*deleting the app never landed on its environment*) fails the same with the JSON path switched off, so it is not this. M6 (R7) — the read path clones a row 3–5 times (scalars, @from, computed, field policy with delete, mirror drop) and include.js carries a second copy of the chain: 0.17 µs/row plain against 0.40 with Json + Boolean + @computed + @omit; one owned clone at the top, the include copy changed in the same commit (FJS-223). M4 (R11) — each nested child is still one full verb, and before FJS-2313 each one also paid an exists() per foreign key | 2026-10-16 | What stood under the pointer is now closed or has a row of its own. M11: getTableStats summed every table's COUNT(*) to price one row, and resolveAllRowCounts called it once per table, so a percent or size limit over T tables ran T + T² counts (156 for 12, measured). It and resolveRowCount now take a plain countRows, and only a bytes limit on one table prices a row (transform/framework.js). test/transform-row-counts.test.ts goes red at HEAD and green here. M5 was closed 2026-10-10. M12's remaining half is FJS-2291, blocked by FJS-D849; advise's retention-without-an-index already covers a model that is not soft-deleted. M6 (R7, row cloning) is FJS-3001 and M4 (R11, one statement per nested child) is FJS-3002. litestone test 7508/0 and statements ratchet green; sierra test:safety and the studio drives pass; the example drives could not start because port 8110 already answered; basecamp verify asks for --reset on a dev db holding 5 users, and transform/ is in neither app's path · [PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md](packages/litestone/bench/PERFORMANCE_AUDIT.md) · [FJS-112](ISSUES.md#fjs-112) |

| <a id="fjs-555"></a>FJS-555 | cli · basecamp — **`example/site` and `example/widgets` build from a context holding a real `.env` with no `.dockerignore` at all.** Retitled 2026-09-13 — basecamp's half is fixed and what follows is how the class was found. Filed as: a `.dockerignore` pattern without `**` protects the context ROOT and nothing under it, so basecamp shipped a stray SQLite database into its image. Docker matches an ignore pattern with Go's `filepath.Match`, where a plain `*` does not cross a separator — measured: with `.env.*`, a root `.env.production` is excluded and `api/.env.production` is **copied**; `**/.env.*` reaches both. basecamp's file said `db/*.db`, which excluded `db/basecamp.db` and admitted `db/db/basecamp.db` — and `db/db/` is precisely what a relative `database { path }` resolved against the wrong working directory creates ([FJS-449](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-449)), git-ignored, so it appears in no diff. The Dockerfile does `COPY db ./db` and then `COPY --from=build /app /app`, so it reached the final image; `fli deploy:local` on a developer's machine therefore built an image carrying that machine's database, which is the exact hazard the file's own comment says it is guarding against. **The pattern is fixed and the class is now checked** — `fli deploy`'s `02b-build-check` step grades this over the server's real build context and refuses. **That claim was half true and is corrected 2026-08-29**: the check's classifier (`isStateFile`) graded `.db-wal` and `.db-shm` as state, and its finder (`CONTEXT_FIND`) looked for `*.db` and not the sidecars — two lists for one fact, written twice, disagreeing, with the finder's own comment claiming it was *the same list spelled for `find`*. So SQLite's sidecars were invisible to the rule that exists to catch them, and the SCAFFOLD's own `.dockerignore` still said `db/*.db`. The consequence was measured on a real deploy: the container writes `db/app.db-wal` into the mounted volume, which is inside the build context, so **every deploy after the first copied the running app's write-ahead log into the image** — one deployment's live data in the artefact, and a moving image digest, which under `04c-journal` made an unchanged redeploy mint a new Release. The finder is now built from the classifier's list and a test asserts they agree; the scaffold writes the `**/` forms basecamp already had. What is left is the other apps: `example/site` and `example/widgets` build from an `example/` context holding a real `.env`, with no `.dockerignore` at all, and both are reported as a warning because their runtime stages copy subtrees rather than the whole — the value stops in an intermediate layer on the build host, readable with `docker build --target build`, rather than shipping | 2026-10-15 | Added example/.dockerignore (**/.env, **/.env.*, !**/.env.example, **/dist, node_modules, job queue, audit trail, db write-ahead sidecars) at the context root both site/deploy and widgets/deploy build from, so the real .env no longer reaches the build stage; the site's data stays in the context because its prerender load() reads it at build time. Proved by packages/cli/test/build-check.test.js 'example/.dockerignore' (red with the file emptied, green with it), which grades the real file and both real Dockerfiles through inspectBuild. · [build-check.js](packages/cli/core/build-check.js) · [.dockerignore](packages/basecamp/.dockerignore) |

| <a id="fjs-1028"></a>FJS-1028 | cli — **`test/server.test.js` asserts that a well-known DEV port is unbound, so five rows go red whenever anybody is developing.** `a tool moves down → up → down as something binds its port` takes `rows.find(r => r.kind === 'tool')` and opens with `expect(await at()).toBe('down')`; the four `GET /api/health/:id` rows below it start a server on that same port. Is port 8503 in use?`. **The suite is green only when nobody is working.** It is the repo's own formula read backwards — env 7 is test, env 8 is dev, and a test asserting about ports belongs on the 7 tier — but the tools block is DEFINED as dev/tooling/project-0 and reserved whole, so the rows genuinely carry 8500-series numbers and the fix is not a digit swap. **What earns it a row rather than a note is the direction it fails in**: loudly, locally, and looking exactly like a real regression. Measured three times in one session — twice inside a CI verdict that was otherwise green, once while grading an unrelated change to `02-publish-all` — and each time it cost a fresh investigation to rule out. `FLI_PORT` is already overridden to `13141` at the top of this same file, so the precedent for isolating a port here exists and was not extended to the rows that most need it. | <a id="fjs-1050"></a>FJS-1050 | css — **The vocabulary's both-directions check exempts a term whose class is `null`, so a term with NEITHER an element nor a class is graded by nothing — which is how `Group` shipped no CSS for its whole life.** Found 2026-09-08 ruling [FJS-D252](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d252). `vocabClass` returns `row[3]` where the row has one and the lowercased term otherwise ([vocabulary.js:712](packages/css/vocabulary.js#L712)), and the forward test returns early on `t.cls === null` with the reason *carried by an element; nothing to find* ([vocabulary.spec.js:62](packages/css/test/specs/vocabulary.spec.js#L62)). **The exemption is correct for the case it was written for and wrong for the one beside it**: `Section` is `<section>` and needs no class, while `Group` was declared `<div>` — an element that conveys nothing — so *carried by an element* was false and the term could not be written at all. It was named in the vocabulary, routed by the decision wizard, and rendered nowhere. **The distinguishing fact is in the row already**: a `null` class beside a SEMANTIC element is a term the browser carries, and a `null` class beside `<div>` is a term with no way to exist. So the check can grade it — a `null` class is legitimate only where `element` is not a bare `<div>` — which is a condition rather than a new list, and the reason this is filed rather than left as a note. Fixed for Group by shipping `.group`; every other `null`-class term is ungraded until the condition lands | 2026-10-14 | The forward vocabulary check returned early on any null class, so a term with no class beside a bare <div> was graded by nothing. vocabulary.spec.js now fails a null-class term whose element is <div>; proved red by setting Text's element to <div> (1 failing), green on the real vocabulary (css suite 553 passing). Also corrected vocabulary.js header, which still called Group structural. · [vocabulary.spec.js](packages/css/test/specs/vocabulary.spec.js) · [vocabulary.js `vocabClass`](packages/css/vocabulary.js#L711) · [FJS-D252](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d252) |

| <a id="fjs-d908"></a>FJS-D908 | litestone — **How does a per-row zone (a column, possibly two relations away) reach a where: a lowered zone-aware operator, a materialized instant, or a framework-bound per-zone window?** | 2026-10-13 | Ruled [`FJS-D908`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d908): **A** — a zone-aware operator the client lowers: the caller states the wall-clock rule and the zone field (`{ startsAt: { localTime: { atOrBefore: '08:00', zone: 'inviteeTimeZone' } } }`); litestone selects the distinct zones present (`SELECT DISTINCT zone`, bounded and indexable), computes each zone's instant bound with `fromWall`/`partsIn`, and lowers to `(zone = ? AND startsAt <= ?) OR …`. SQL stays instant-only, so `FJS-D143` stands and the cost is one DISTINCT plus an index range per zone. The zone must be a column of the same row; a zone two relations away (`Shift → Employee → User`) needs a join the lowering does not do today, so that case stays open or is solved by A + a denormalized zone column. Adds an operator to `where`, `$checkWhere` and the directive table. · [IDEAS/owed-rulings.md](IDEAS/owed-rulings.md) |

| <a id="fjs-1409"></a>FJS-1409 | conduit — **A request's own `timeout_ms` is graded as the target's fault, so one impatient caller opens a healthy target's breaker for every caller of that conduit.** `timeout` is in `TARGET_FAULTS` whichever timer produced it: the target's declared `timeout_ms`, or a shorter one the CALLER put on the request. **Measured** 2026-09-27 in *Portal, the search stressor*. A target declares no timeout, so its 600 ms answer is fine by its own policy. Five sends with `timeout_ms: 100` give five `timeout`s, and the next send, with `timeout_ms: 2000`, answers `circuit_open` (control: the same send on a fresh conduit answered in 600 ms). In the app, a 400 ms search budget sheds the `slow` provider after five queries, and a page that would wait two seconds for it (Phase 4's progressive results) is told `circuit_open … retrying in 24s`. The terminal names a healthy provider *circuit_open*. For the 400 ms caller the skip is what it wants, because a request it will always abandon is spend with no answer, and that is exactly why the skip belongs to that caller: the breaker is per target, the patience is per caller, and conduit cannot tell them apart. Candidate: a timeout shorter than the target's own counts as `other` (trips nothing, clears nothing), or the breaker keys on the target and the caller's timeout together. **Measured beside it, and right**: the breaker does count a budget miss, so `dead` is asked 5 times in 50 and skipped from the sixth, and `flaky` at 100 % likewise; at 30 % it never trips (15 misses in 50, never five in a row). A 20-query burst asks `dead` 20 times before the first fault lands, since the breaker counts completed faults; that is ordinary breaker behavior, bounded by `max_concurrent` **Phase 4, on the page (2026-09-27)**: the progressive page waits 2 s per provider (every target's ceiling) and the terminal sends its 400 ms as each request's `timeout_ms`, over one shared conduit. Driven in Chrome: six terminal searches, then one on the page. The page painted `charlie · circuit_open`, though `charlie` answers every request in 600 ms and the page would have waited for it. So the caller that FJS-1409 predicted is real: the person who chose the patient surface loses a healthy provider because another surface was impatient **Beside it, 2026-09-30:** `FJS-1408` gave the caller a way to be impatient that the breaker does not count, `signal` (a miss answers `aborted`), and Portal's terminal budget now uses it. `req.timeout_ms` still trips the breaker as measured, and that is this row | 2026-10-05 | Cause: send() graded every timeout as a target fault, including one from a request's own timeout_ms shorter than the target's, so one impatient caller opened the target's breaker for everyone. Fix: send() grades such a timeout as other when req.timeout_ms is below the target's declared policy.timeout_ms, else the conduit's, else the 10s default (outwaited + Resilience.declaredTimeout). Proof: two new tests in conduit.test.ts (first red before the fix), and Portal's fanout.test.ts pin flipped to assert the patient send is answered. · [portal api/test/fanout.test.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/api/test/fanout.test.ts) · [portal fakes/bench.ts](../fjs-prototypes/portal/fakes/bench.ts) · [resilience.ts `TARGET_FAULTS`](packages/conduit/src/resilience.ts) · [conduit.ts `send`](packages/conduit/src/conduit.ts) |

| <a id="fjs-710"></a>FJS-710 | conduit — **Conduit's error taxonomy is status-shaped where its consumers need it fault-shaped, and everything `fetch` decides it inherited without deciding.** Umbrella for the remaining conduit findings, `D4` and `D6`. **The taxonomy half is ruled [`FJS-D201`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d201)**: the kind vocabulary and its three columns — retryable, does it trip the breaker, what can a caller do — move to `@frontierjs/toolbelt/fault`, read by conduit, caravan and junction alike; classification stays with whoever saw the failure, since a kit that classified would need a transport. **`conduit-5`** — **withdrawn 2026-09-03, it did not reproduce**: a body shorter than its declared `content-length` does not arrive as a success. The reader RAISES, in all three shapes a server can end early in (graceful FIN, shutdown, RST), and the existing catch already answers a retryable `connection_failed`, which is the right kind. What the original measurement caught is the HARNESS — a `Bun.serve` recorder rewrites a fabricated `content-length` to the real body length, so the client sees a consistent short response and correctly reports success, and the declared length never left the test. Pinned with a raw `Bun.listen`, the only way to send a mismatched one; no guard added, because a length check would be unreachable code carrying a comment about a bug that is not there. **`conduit-6`** — split out and **closed as [`FJS-733`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-733)**: a declined replay now says `retryable: false` and carries `indeterminate`, the header name is `idempotency.header`, and `idempotency.auto` mints a key once per `send()`. **`conduit-7`** — split out and **closed as [`FJS-728`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-728)**: policy is now `TargetDescriptor.policy`, seven numbers falling back field-by-field to the conduit's own, refused by name where a field is unknown. **`conduit-8`** — split out and **closed as [`FJS-742`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-742)**: the junction plugin defaults `trace`, junction carries `traceparent`/`tracestate` on `RequestMeta`, and an upstream trace is continued where there is one. **`conduit-9`**: a credential is a static string with no expiry, refresh or rotation, no OAuth2 client-credentials type, no single-flight in `withCache` (100 concurrent misses made 100 inner calls) and no tenant or caller context, so *each shop's own Stripe key* has no seam under `strategy database`. **`conduit-10`**: response decoding is text-only — charset ignored, binary destroyed, a 200 MB body buffered whole, an 11 MB body over the 10 MiB cap blamed on the caller as `invalid_request`, and `stream()` over http answering `not_implemented`. **`conduit-11`**: `raw: err` on `connection_failed` carries Bun's error whose `path` is the full URL including userinfo, so a password reaches `JSON.stringify(result)` — `redactUrl` in [`FJS-775`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-775)'s kit is the owner for this now, written with this asker in mind; observers receive the whole request body with no redaction hook; and a throwing observer prints a full stack per call. **`conduit-12`** — **half closed 2026-09-03**: `err.code` is surfaced in the message, so a refused port, a bad hostname and a certificate no longer read as one sentence. | <a id="fjs-401"></a>FJS-401 | junction · litestone — **A declared input gets a `type`'s validators and not its transforms, and wiring them naively would make the two boundaries disagree about what is VALID.** `methods: [{ method, input: 'PayOrder' }]` validates a custom method's payload against a `type T { … }` in the seed — required keys, types, `@length`, `@gte`, the author's `x-messages`, all of it. What it does not get is `@trim`/`@lower`/`@upper`/`@slug`: those are enforced in litestone's `applyTransforms` at the Data boundary and are emitted into JSON Schema **nowhere**, so nothing downstream can see them, and a custom method's payload never becomes a model write and therefore never meets them. A `type` whose whole point is a normalized value is silently un-normalized. The reason this is a filed question rather than a small patch is ORDER: litestone transforms BEFORE validating (`client.js:5172`, `applyTransforms` and then `validate`), junction's `FieldDef.transform` runs AFTER (`schema.ts:241`), so `@trim @length(3,12)` on `'  ab  '` fails at the Data boundary and passes through a service — the two would not merely produce different output, they would disagree about what is legal, which is the shape Invariant 4 exists to prevent. Doing it properly is three moves and each has a decision in it: litestone emits the transform names (a new keyword in a document with a committed snapshot and three readers); junction gains a PRE-validation slot rather than reusing `transform`, so nothing existing moves; and the implementations want one owner, which by the shape of `/inflect` and `/directives` is a `@frontierjs/toolbelt` subpath both packages read — `@slug` in particular is not a one-liner anyone should write twice. Sierra would then get client-side transforms for free, which it also does not have today. Measured 2026-08-22 and asserted still-broken in `packages/junction/test/method-input.test.ts` — a transform that starts crossing turns that test red rather than leaving it stale. **Amended 2026-09-28, *Portal, the search stressor* (bangs): it is not only a custom method's input — an ordinary MODEL write through a service meets the same disagreement, at two boundaries before litestone.** `Bang.trigger String @lower @regex("^[a-z0-9]{1,12}$")`. Litestone alone does what `fli db:explain @lower` says (*lowercase before validation*): `SYS1` as system and `USR1` as a user both stored as `sys1`/`usr1`, measured. But `POST /api/bangs { trigger: 'UP1' }` answers **400 `trigger: trigger format is invalid`** from junction's `validateField` (`schema.ts`), whose `def.lowercase` exists and is set by nothing because the JSON Schema carries no transform. And the generated `<Form>` refuses first, in Chrome: *trigger is not in the expected format* under the box, `aria-invalid`, no request sent (sierra `field-rules.js`, the `pattern` rule). So the row's premise that a model write *meets* the transforms holds only for a caller that bypasses the service: a person typing `W` in the generated form for a `@lower` trigger cannot save it, and the error blames the format. Any `@trim`/`@lower`/`@upper` beside `@regex`, `@length` or `@startsWith` is exposed; `@trim @length` on `' ab '` is the row's own example, now reachable from a form. Pinned in portal `api/test/bangs.test.ts` (*FJS-401 pin*: the service's 400 beside litestone's lowering, green while this is open); D482's decision now has a model-write caller and a form | 2026-10-04 | Cause: litestone applied @trim/@lower/@upper/@slug before validating but emitted them into JSON Schema nowhere, so junction (service payloads, declared method inputs, model writes) and sierra (generated forms) graded the raw value and disagreed about what is valid. Fix per FJS-D482 A: one owner, @frontierjs/toolbelt/transforms (transform/isTransform/TRANSFORM_NAMES), which litestone's transformValue now calls; litestone emits ordered x-transforms from applyValidators (columns and type fields); junction reads it into FieldDef.transforms and runs it ahead of the checks in validateField (FieldDef.transform unchanged, still post-validation); sierra carries x-transforms and applies it at the top of _checkConstraints. Proof: toolbelt transforms.spec.js, litestone messages.test.ts, junction method-input.test.ts (the old still-broken pin flipped to assert trim reaches the method and the trimmed length is what is graded; red with the read stubbed), sierra field-messages.test.js (red with the call stubbed); suites green in toolbelt, litestone, junction (plus typecheck clean) and sierra; example verify:widget green. · [client.js:5172](packages/litestone/src/core/client.js#L5172) · [schema.ts:241](packages/junction/src/core/schema.ts#L241) · [jsonschema.js](packages/litestone/src/jsonschema.js) |
| <a id="fjs-659"></a>FJS-659 | junction · conduit — **Junction's mail battery re-hand-rolls the ring conduit exists to own, and it ships a second credential convention while doing it.** `createResendMailer` (`src/mail/index.ts`) holds a raw `apiKey` in a closure, hardcodes `https://api.resend.com`, and calls `fetch` with **no retry, no timeout, no deadline, no breaker, no observers and no line in `/metrics`**. Dialing out directly is CORRECT and is not the defect — `IMail` is a contract with a working default, which is what keeps `@frontierjs/conduit` optional, and the escalation path already exists in both directions (`packages/basecamp/api/src/core/mailer.ts` is `IMail` over `app.conduit`; junction's email CAMPAIGN tier refuses to run without conduit and says so by name). **What is wrong is the second convention**: conduit's rule is that a target carries a credential *reference* and material is resolved at send time so it stays out of the registry, out of hooks and off the management routes, and this adapter takes the secret itself as a constructor argument — so one framework teaches two incompatible habits about the most sensitive value an integration holds. The narrow fix is a shared resilient `fetch` helper plus a ref-shaped credential option; the wide one is a conduit-backed default when `app.conduit` is present. **It was two adapters and is now one, which is the precedent rather than a shrunken scope**: the AI half named `createAnthropicModel` and an OpenAI-shaped adapter, and both were DELETED by [FJS-903](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-903) / [FJS-D215](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d215) rather than fixed, on the ground that a connector to a named vendor does not live in a boundary package ([FJS-D153](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d153)). Proved by test/resend-credentials.test.ts (red before, green after), junction test (2561 pass) and typecheck clean; the drives are not mail-bound and fli prove's failures (example verify, basecamp verify needing --reset, verify:live open FJS-1382/FJS-1371) read as shared-port/DB state. · [mail/index.ts:153](packages/junction/src/mail/index.ts#L153) · [credentials.ts](packages/conduit/src/credentials.ts) · [FJS-D177](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d177) · [FJS-D215](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d215) · [FJS-D219](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d219) |

| <a id="fjs-d566"></a>FJS-D566 | litestone — **How does a row policy say *the caller is one of this row's members* — a to-many test `rel.any(…)` compiled as a correlated EXISTS, or a `claim … from` that yields a list read with `in`?** | 2026-09-30 | Ruled [`FJS-D566`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d566): **A** — a to-many test in the policy language: `<hasMany>.any(<expr>)`, where `<expr>` names only the CHILD's columns and `auth()`. | <a id="fjs-598"></a>FJS-598 | repo · litestone — **The tool built to find holes in the checks runs in CI only over a tutorial's schema — neither app's is ever mutated.** Corrected 2026-09-13: the `tutor` phase (full tier only) ends `tutor:test` with `litestone mutate` over the lesson's own schema (`commands/tutor/_steps-test/05-mutate.md`), so the tool is proven to RUN and nothing grades `example` or `basecamp` with it. `litestone mutate` mutates the SCHEMA and runs the checks derived from the ORIGINAL against a database built from the mutant, so a surviving mutant is a statement about the SUITE rather than about the schema — and every survivor it has reported so far named a check that did not exist yet and now does (`verifyGateLadder`, `verifyConstraints`, `verifyFieldProtection` and `verifyRowPolicies` are each in the default set because a mutant survived without one). Nothing re-asks the question after a schema changes, so a `@@gate` added to a model no fixture reaches is ungraded and silent, which is the same shape as a snapshot that stops being checked. **What has to be decided before a phase exists is the tier, and it is measured**: `example` scores **100% — 159/159 graded in 239s**, 15 of them refused by the parser or the loader and the other 144 killed by a verdict disagreement. `basecamp` is 328 mutants, runnable since [FJS-597](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md#fjs-597) and needing `ENCRYPTION_KEY` in the environment — and it does NOT scale from example's rate: a full run was still going at **25 minutes** when it was killed. The per-mutant cost is a property of the SCHEMA rather than of the tool, and basecamp's is the expensive shape — 45 models, 34 of them carrying row policies, under declared row tenancy, so `verifyRowPolicies` and `verifyTenantIsolation` are grading a far larger surface per mutant than example's 26 models ask for. So the pair is well past half an hour and a pre-push tier costing ~40s is out by two orders of magnitude. Full tier, a nightly, or a `--kinds` subset on the fast one. **The 100% is the argument FOR the phase rather than against it**: the four checks already see everything this schema can express, so a phase added today starts green and fires the first time somebody declares something they cannot see — which is precisely the ratchet, and precisely what nobody notices without one. So a score BASELINE is the other half, the way `scripts/typecheck-baselines.json` is (Invariant 14): a phase that fails on any survivor fails on the first schema anybody adds, and a phase that prints a percentage nobody reads is the `access` phase's problem without the `access` phase's excuse. | 2026-09-30 | CI now has a full-tier `mutate` phase (scripts/ci.mjs) running `litestone mutate --json` over example and basecamp and failing a score below each app's floor in scripts/mutate-baselines.json, which ratchets up (FJS-D476). Both run under a five-kind subset (deny/encrypted/guarded-drop, relator-loosen/tighten): measured, a mutant costs ~30s and example is ~490 mutants. Floors are measured, not assumed: example 17/17 = 100 in 5m, basecamp 14/22 = 64 in ~11m; its survivors are FJS-1594 and the new deny-drop row. · [ci.mjs](scripts/ci.mjs) · [mutate.js](packages/litestone/src/mutate.js) · [test/mutate.md](packages/cli/commands/test/mutate.md) |

| <a id="fjs-1278"></a>FJS-1278 | sierra · junction · litestone — **A replayed write reaches the boundary with no statement of WHEN it was made, so a server that stamps `now()` dates a whole shift's work at the moment the network came back.** **Wants a ruling, not only a fix.** | 2026-09-29 | Built to FJS-D469. | <a id="fjs-1419"></a>FJS-1419 | junction · sierra — **A live list re-asks the query of the last load that ANSWERED whenever it refetches, so a `changed` announcement (any bulk write, any sweep) or a reconnect resync that lands while a newer load is in flight re-issues the superseded query, is the newest load, and wins: the store holds the old query's rows, and every push after it is judged against the old query.** `refetch` calls `load(lastQuery, lastParams)`, and `lastQuery` is set only when a load's answer is written (`FJS-082`'s stamp, which makes the LAST ISSUED load the one that writes). **Seen** 2026-09-27 on *Portal, the search stressor*'s search page, spelling B of PLAN.md Q2 (a search's hits as rows in a live list whose filter moves to each new run). From the tenth minute of a drive the page painted 0 of 20 hits for whole searches, while the run completed: that is when the first rows expired, so `searchRows`' `deleteMany({ onlyExpired: true })` announced `searchHits changed` in the same few milliseconds the page moved the list to the new run. The dev log shows the tell, two `find searchHits` 3 ms apart. **Measured** with the browser's own client over HTTP (pinned): `load({ runId: old })`, then `load({ runId: new })` and a `changed` while it is in flight. The new load answers the new run's row, and the store holds the old run's. Through sierra's `list()`, the page's `match` then refuses the new run's pushed rows as outside the old query, so nothing arrives until the next load. Nothing is logged. Any list whose filter changes as the person types, beside any writer doing bulk writes, is exposed. Fix: record the query when a load is ISSUED (the query the store is moving to) and have `refetch` ask that, or have a refetch that finds a load in flight wait for it and re-ask its query **Amended 2026-09-27, *Portal, the search stressor* Phase 5: the pin raced, and now holds.** Phase 4's pin asserted that the STORE ends on the old run. Run alone, it went red in 1 of 3, and in 4 of 8 once it was changed to assert what the server was asked. The refetch reads `lastQuery` when it fires, so whether it re-asks the superseded query depends on whether the newer load has already answered. The pin now holds the newer load's `find` open for 150 ms on the server, which is the page's condition made certain, and asserts the server was asked `[new, old]`: 8 of 8. Which answer the store then keeps is the order the two responses land in, so it is not pinned | 2026-09-28 | refetch re-asked lastQuery, which is stamped only when a load's answer writes the store, so a changed announcement or a reconnect resync that landed during a newer load re-issued the superseded query as the newest load, and it won. load() now records the query and directives it ISSUES (issuedQuery/issuedParams), and refetch asks those. lastQuery stays the store's own query for match and more(). test/client.test.ts 'a changed event during a newer load re-asks the newer query' asserted the server was asked [old, new, old] before the fix and asks [old, new, new] with the store on new after it. The junction suite passes, 2453 tests. | <a id="fjs-1108"></a>FJS-1108 | litestone — **A single-row `update()` still cost more than on 2026-08-18 once the transaction wrapper was off it, and the rest was not the wrapper.** | 2026-09-13 | **Fixed, all but a residual with no single cause.** Remeasured on a quiet machine, `model User { id Int @id; name String; age Int }`, one `Int` set by id, best of eight interleaved: **11.61 µs at `4f46e5b`, 15.95 before, 13.18 after**; bytes allocated per update, read off the collector, **6,857 / 9,155 / 7,635**. Two causes, found apart. **Most of it was `writeData` outgrowing the optimizer**: 5,805 bytecodes at `4f46e5b`, 11,171 before — the `@@extensible` blocks, the `@guarded`/`@system`/`@immutable` refusals and their wording, the required and clearing checks, encryption, enums and the unbindable-value check, all inline and none of them reached by an ordinary write. With the optimizing tiers off the two trees were 15% apart, which is what instruction counts said; with DFG on they were 40% apart. The cold blocks are named functions in the same closure now and their conditions stay in `writeData`, which is 3,362 bytecodes. **The rest was work paid for options the call did not pass**: the guard sequence cost ~29K instructions an update against ~11K at `4f46e5b`, most of it `checkOrderBy`, `checkSelect` and `checkTakeSkip` building their answers for an absent `orderBy`, `select` or `take` — each now returns first, inside itself, which is 8K instructions dearer than skipping the call in `guardArgs` and keeps one statement of when a check has nothing to do. `enforceValueSets` answers `undefined` rather than an async function's promise for a model binding no set, `setFragment` binds directly where the model has no field-write policy, and `stampSets` takes the column list rather than a `Set` built for a model with no stamp. **What is left** — +14% on update, +8% on `create()` by the same clock — is spread across the features added since, each under ~5K instructions or ~200 bytes when stubbed, which is below what either instrument resolves. **Instruction counts disagreed with the fix**: 273.9K / 314.2K / 323.4K, worse after it, because a 1,000-update count grades code the optimizer has not reached and the split adds calls there — recorded in `IDEAS/performance-regression-watch.md`. litestone 4,795 pass, junction 2,356, sierra `test:safety` 12/12, typecheck clean |
| <a id="fjs-1107"></a>FJS-1107 | litestone — **A single-row `update()` cost 114% more than on 2026-08-18, behind the same transaction wrapper `FJS-1106` took off `create()`.** | 2026-09-13 | **Fixed, the wrapper half.** An update with no nested or edge write, no `post-update` policy, no `@@transitions` and **no transaction open** runs its body without `tx.exclusive`. Those three keep it because each is a different reason: more statements, a refusal that IS the rollback, and a move graded across an await. The nested belongsTo write and `checkTransitions` are awaited only when they have work, so on this path nothing yields before the statement. **The update checks that before it writes**: one that chose to run alone and finds a transaction open throws, naming `FJS-1107`, instead of joining it — so an await added ahead of the statement later is a loud defect, not a lost write. `test/write-autocommit.test.ts` (renamed from the create-only file, which was also fixed: its *was BEGIN prepared* probe stopped meaning anything once one transaction had cached it) reads `inTransaction` on the raw connection as each statement executes. Its concurrent update case fails with the depth check removed — through the guard's own error — and fails again with the guard removed too. Clock, best of six under heavy load: 14.33 µs at `4f46e5b`, 28.48 before, 20.86 after; instruction counts 223.9K / 327.7K / 260.7K. **What is left is not the wrapper** — [FJS-1108](#fjs-1108). litestone 4,795 pass, junction 2,356, sierra `test:safety` 12/12, typecheck clean |
| <a id="fjs-1106"></a>FJS-1106 | litestone — **A single-row `create()` cost 82% more than on 2026-08-18, because every create took the transaction lock, an async scope and a `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`/`COMMIT` pair — including the create that is one INSERT and was already atomic.** | 2026-09-13 | **Fixed.** Bisected by instruction count to `3f38d4b`, where `FJS-638` wrapped the create body in `tx.exclusive`. Everything else keeps the transaction. `wrapDb` also caches `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` — its comment said reuse throws across transaction boundaries, and a prepared one was measured reused across 1,000 commits, rollbacks, a failed statement and a thrown COMMIT on `:memory:` and on a WAL file; `SAVEPOINT`/`RELEASE`/`ROLLBACK TO` stay out because their names count up. | <a id="fjs-1087"></a>FJS-1087 | example · junction — **A signed-in shopper can mark any invoice paid and change any customer's subscription, because a custom method's floor checks presence and both bodies write through `asSystem()` before reading anything as the caller.** | 2026-09-12 | Measured 2026-09-12 over HTTP against a throwaway tenant, as `robin@buyer.test` (a verified shopper, USER(4) — the same rung as staff, `example/db/user.lite` § Who is staff) against rows belonging to another customer: `GET /invoices/:id` answered **404** and `POST /invoices/:id` with `X-Service-Method: settle` answered **204** and left the invoice `paid`; `GET /subscriptions/:id` answered **404** and `changePlan { quantity: 7 }` answered **200**, moved the quantity, and ISSUED a proration invoice (`INV-3002`, 14400) against that customer. Anonymous callers are refused 401 and staff are the paired control (200 both). **The mechanism is correct behavior composed wrongly.** `FJS-826`'s floor is the model's read gate and is a presence check by design — `find` is graded at the Data boundary, so re-grading the level here would be a second reading ([litestone.ts `gateAuthAround`](packages/junction/src/core/litestone.ts)). That holds for a body that reads as the caller: `payRuns.*`, `inventory.receive`/`adjust`, `orders.refund` and `invoices.void` all do, and a shopper gets a 404 or a 403 from them. `invoices.settle` and `subscriptions.changePlan` go straight to `asSystem()`, where no row policy and no gate sees who asked. **The instrument now exists**: `surface.snapshot.md` prints who may call each custom method and lists every one whose caller's standing is not graded — 35 in `example`, 110 in `basecamp`, the second untriaged. **A sibling gap the same reading found**: a declared `methods: [{ method, gate }]` level is enforced only when the service's model declares `@@gate`; on a modelless service `gateAuth` reads null levels and checks nothing, the declaration included. **Two fixes and they are different claims.** In the app, each method either declares the level it needs or reads its row through `$.db` before `asSystem()` — which level `settle` needs is a policy call, since `void` is `@gate(5)` and staff grade 4. In the framework, the floor could compare the caller's level to the read gate rather than their presence, which would not close either hole here (both models read at 1) and would re-open `FJS-826`'s ruling. `@frontierjs/mcp`'s `move-system` verdict reads `settle` as *no caller* and is wrong in the same place. **`example`'s two holes are closed, 2026-09-12, and no level could have closed `settle`**: staff and a verified shopper both grade 4, so *staff* is a predicate. `Invoice` is `@@gate("1.8.4.8")` with `@@allow('update', auth().isStaff)`, `customerId` and `subscriptionId` gained `@immutable` so an update reaches only the moves, and `settle` stays `@system` — `@system` on a move is `transition(id, name, { system: true })` on the CALLER's client (`FJS-D150`), so `settleInvoice` runs on staff's client and the policy grades who pressed. `changePlan` reads the subscription through `$.db` before `asSystem()`, and its read and update policies name the same two callers (staff, owner). Re-measured on a throwaway tenant: robin settling another customer's invoice **404** and her own **403**, staff **200** with `paidAt` stamped; robin's `changePlan` on another customer's subscription **404** with no invoice issued, on her own **200**, staff **200**. `void` moved with it: behind update 8 it was reachable by nobody, and at update 4 an admin voids (**200**) and staff are refused at the move's `@gate(5)` (**403**). **A per-move predicate — `settle: issued -> paid @allow(auth().isStaff)` — was weighed and not built**: a move is an update underneath, so `@@allow('update', …)` already grades it, and two moves at one rung needing different callers is `@@capabilities`' grid (`FJS-D139`, `FJS-D149`); a third spelling would be a second origin. Measured before the app edit on a schema with no new syntax. Reading each invoice as the caller first also hides [FJS-1093](#fjs-1093) at this app. **Basecamp's 110 triaged, 2026-09-12**: each method read for whether a system client or a guarded write is reached before anything grades the caller, and every suspect run on the real app through `@frontierjs/testing` rather than taken from the reading. **~103 are graded by something the snapshot cannot see** — `sessionScope` (authenticate → a workspace is required → membership, so `requireWorkspaceRole`'s silent return on an empty workspace never fires behind it), a role hook, `internalOnly`, `requireSystemAdmin`, a `getScoped` read before `sys()`, or a write through the scoped client. **Four were holes, all measured open and now closed**: `workspaces.members` read any workspace's roster through `asSystem()` with `include: { user: true }`, so an account in no workspace got every member's whole `User` row, `isSystemAdmin` included, while `get` on the same id answered 404 — it checks membership first now; `GET`/`DELETE /conduit-targets` sat behind `authenticate` alone, so any account listed every workspace's outpost and channel targets and deregistered another workspace's machine — it is `requireSystemAdmin()` now, and API keys were already refused it; `environments.setVariable`/`deleteVariable` skipped the protected-environment refusal `patch` makes, and the capability grid cannot say it because a developer holds `Environment.variables` everywhere — measured, a developer set production's `DATABASE_URL` — one `refuseProtectedForDeveloper` reads for all three writers now; and every `restore` was graded by nothing at all, which is a litestone defect rather than basecamp's ([FJS-1096](#fjs-1096)). `api/test/services.test.ts` § *a custom method grades its caller*, four tests, each refusal paired with the caller it must still admit. **`example`'s two closes are pinned, 2026-09-12**: `verify:account` asks `settle` and `changePlan` as robin of another customer's rows (404, nothing moved, no document issued) and of her own invoice (403), each paired with staff on the same row (200) — with both service bodies put back to `asSystem()` first, 4 of its 44 rows red and the run reproduces the original 204 and the issued invoice. **The declared gate on a modelless service is graded, 2026-09-12**: `customMethodGrade` reads the declaration before the model, `test/custom-method-gate.test.ts` drives a service over no model (3 of 18 red with the old order). **`move-system` is gone, 2026-09-12**: `@system` is whose decision a move is, not how senior (`FJS-D150`), so it grades `move-floor`; over `example` the tools withheld from everybody went from 4 to none. **The snapshot's list is split by what stands in front of the body, 2026-09-12**: a row with only the floor in front is listed apart from one an app hook runs in front of, and that hook is named — the snapshot cannot read a hook or a body, so it says what runs rather than calling either graded. Basecamp's thirteen hook factories returned arrows and rendered `anonymous`; each returns a function named for itself now (132 `anonymous` → 6, all app-level or inline). Over the two apps: `example` 19 bare and 17 hooked, `basecamp` 11 bare and 100 hooked, and every bare row is an auth `account` method that grades inside its body, a `restore` graded at the Data boundary since `FJS-1096`, or one of `example`'s billing methods that `verify:account` now pins. `test/surface-snapshot.test.ts` asserts the split, and counting the derived hooks as hooks in front reds it. · [invoices.service.ts `settle`](example/api/src/services/invoices.service.ts) · [subscriptions.service.ts `changePlan`](example/api/src/services/subscriptions.service.ts) · [surface.snapshot.md](example/api/surface.snapshot.md) · [basecamp surface.snapshot.md](packages/basecamp/surface.snapshot.md) · [FJS-826](#fjs-826) · [IDEAS/run-intent-recognizer-1.md](IDEAS/run-intent-recognizer-1.md) A24 |

| <a id="fjs-1076"></a>FJS-1076 | litestone — **The only object-store signer in the framework had no test, and two defects found by reading it were real: a key with a space or a non-ASCII letter was signed double-encoded, and a query was signed unsorted** | 2026-09-12 | **Graded by AWS rather than by itself.** Ten cases of AWS's own SigV4 suite (`awslabs/aws-c-auth`, pinned commit, Apache-2.0) are vendored under `test/fixtures/sigv4/` and run header-signed and presigned; beside them, the three worked examples from AWS's S3 documentation, which the old signer already passed and which are the half that had to stay green. Against the old code 21 of 27 failed, each for a named reason: `/example space/` canonicalized as `/example%2520space/`, `Param2` before `Param1`, and the S3-only payload handling applied to every service. **The fix is three rules with one owner each** in `sigv4.js`: `uriEncode` (AWS's unreserved set, once), `canonicalUri` (decode each segment, encode again — S3 re-derives the path from the decoded key, so the canonical form is built from the key and never from `URL.pathname`), `canonicalQuery` (encoded, then sorted). What remains: a key segment that is exactly `.` or `..` is still collapsed by the URL parser, which no keyPattern produces; and the three public-URL builders disagree, filed as [FJS-1094](ISSUES.md#fjs-1094). | <a id="fjs-882"></a>FJS-882 | mesa — **The parser knew where it was the whole time and the failures did not say.** | 2026-09-07 | One `Reader` runs over the whole source — `new Reader(r)` returns `r`, so the index is always absolute — and every node carries `start`. Three shapes spent it. **The generic reader failure carried no position at all**: `Wrong syntax at:` plus thirty raw bytes taken straight off the offset, newlines included, so the quoted fragment ran past the end of the line and held source the failure had nothing to do with. Four different malformed inputs land there — an unterminated close tag, an unterminated comment, a doctype, a processing instruction — and none of them named a line. It quotes one line now and carries the offset. **A close tag that matches nothing reported the CLOSE tag's line, which is the line the author wrote correctly.** The message already named the construct still open, which was the previous pass at this; what it could not do was say WHERE that construct was opened, and that is the line to go to. It says both now. **And `<ul><li>a<li>b</ul>` is valid HTML.** Mesa refuses it — a language choice, and a defensible one, since an implicit close is a rule about where a tag ends that the author cannot see in the file — but the refusal said nothing about the choice, so somebody who had written correct HTML was told only that something was still open. The extra sentence fires for the twenty-odd elements HTML lets you omit and for nothing else, because a paragraph about end tags under an unclosed `{#if}` is noise at the moment somebody is reading carefully. Stated in `VISION.md` § 10 and as rule 29b, which is the half the row said no document held. **CDATA is named rather than supported.** `<![CDATA[ … ]]>` in an `<svg>` subtree read as `Wrong syntax at: ![CDATA[ x < y ]]>`, which is a fragment to search for. It arrives by copy-paste out of an exporter's SVG, so the message says what to do with the paste — drop the wrapper, write `&lt;`, `&amp;` and `&lbrace;` — and the test compiles that advice rather than quoting it, since an entity that the compiler swallowed would make the sentence a lie. **Supporting it was considered and refused**: it is legal in XML and in HTML foreign content, and a Mesa template is neither, so accepting it means deciding whether `{` interpolates inside one, which is a language feature and not a diagnostic. Filed as [FJS-966](ISSUES.md#fjs-966). **Svelte is the comparison on all three and it lands differently on each.** On the close tag it points at the CLOSE tag and never at both — [#16628](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/16628) is exactly the complaint that the reported line is the one the author wrote correctly, closed the same day with no change — so naming the open position is ahead of it rather than catching up. On CDATA it has no handling at all: `grep -i cdata` over the compiler is zero hits and `<![CDATA[` falls through to `tag_invalid_name`, *Expected a valid element or component name*, which is the same shape of miss. On implicit closing it went the other way and then walked it back — it implements the WHATWG omission table, and since 5.32 it WARNS on every implicit close it performs ([#12635](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/issues/12635), [PR #15932](https://github.com/sveltejs/svelte/pull/15932)): *can cause an unexpected DOM structure. Add an explicit `</li>` to avoid surprises*. The sharper evidence is that Svelte 5 silently LOST the case Svelte 3 added the feature for: `<ul>&#123;#if x&#125;<li>a&#123;/if&#125;</ul>` compiles on 4.2.20 and is a `block_unexpected_close` on 5.57, the original fixture gone and no issue filed. A rule subtle enough to regress unnoticed inside the compiler that owns it is not one an author can hold, which is the argument for the refusal and is now in `VISION.md` beside it. 21 tests, measured against each mechanism separately — 4 red without the CDATA branch, 4 without the reader offset, 2 without the opened-at position, 5 without the omittable-tag sentence. | <a id="fjs-898"></a>FJS-898 | junction — **Two cache drivers behind one interface disagreed twelve ways, and swapping the driver was the only way to find out** | 2026-09-05 | `batteries-9`. An interface exists so a caller need not know which backend answers, and every difference here was a way that promise was false — measured before anything changed: a memory `get()` handed back the STORED reference (mutating the row a caller had already `set` changed what the cache held, and so did mutating what `get` answered) where sqlite round-tripped; `undefined` and a function stored in memory and threw a NOT NULL in sqlite; a **Date came back a Date from one and a string from the other**, a `Map` a `Map` and a `{}`, `NaN` itself and `null`; `clear()` answered a count and 0; `clear(pattern)` was a SUBSTRING match in memory and a PREFIX in sqlite; eviction was FIFO. **The fix is one codec both drivers call, not a fix per driver** — that is what makes a thirteenth divergence unreachable rather than unfiled. What a cache value may be is DERIVED and not chosen: JSON is what a Litestone row already is (a `DateTime` reads back an ISO string, measured), what a response body carries and what a WS frame carries, so the cache holds what the wire holds and owes no rule of its own. What JSON would LOSE is refused at `set()` naming the key and the way out — a Date says store the ISO string, a BigInt says store digits the way `Int @big` crosses — and the walk is the one `JSON.stringify` was already doing, so grading costs no second pass. `undefined` is refused for a second reason: `get()` answers it for a miss, so a stored one could not be read back, which is also what makes `getOrSet`'s miss check sound. **The memory driver holds the value ENCODED**, which is what buys value semantics: a shared reference is a semantics no persistent backend can offer, so code written against it breaks on the day the driver is swapped. Eviction is LRU with `get()` a use and `has()` deliberately not one, an overwrite re-inserting because `Map.set` on an existing key does not move it. `getOrSet` is the read-through with single flight — one factory run per key however many callers arrive, a rejection reaching all of them and cached for none. **The conformance suite is the artefact and it found the twelfth on its first run**: sqlite escaped `%` and `_` with a backslash and declared no `ESCAPE`, so a prefix containing either matched nothing. Where it disagreed was GC: HikariCP, Go's `database/sql` and pgbouncer all evict idle entries only and retire a busy one **when it is returned**, and the `FinalizationRegistry` proposal itself says not to rely on cleanup callbacks — which is what put the lease in junction rather than trusting collection. **The new tests caught two bugs in the fix**: the cold ring defaulted to the fan-out concurrency (8) with no cap, so on any pool smaller than that it could never fill, never recycled, and every cold insert evicted a hot entry — scan resistance silently off for exactly the small pools that need it; and the recycle threshold was `>` where the victim is chosen before the insert, letting the ring grow a slot per insert. | <a id="fjs-638"></a>FJS-638 | litestone — **Single-row writes and every read bypassed the transaction machinery: dirty reads, ghost writes, torn nested writes, a fake rollback, and rolled-back rows broadcast to every open tab** | 2026-09-01 | Five symptoms, one cause: [`FJS-237`](ISSUES_ARCHIVE.md) built the FIFO lock and the AsyncLocalStorage ownership and only `$transaction`, `createMany` and `upsertMany` ever acquired them. **All four measured before and after.** *(a)* The read router picked its connection off a GLOBAL `txState.depth`, so while any transaction was open anywhere every read in the process went to the write connection and saw uncommitted rows — it asks `ownsTx()` now, the same question `wrapExclusive` asks to spot a genuine nesting, so the two cannot disagree about who is inside. *(b)* Every write verb now runs its database region through the lock — `create` and `update` through `exclusive` (their nested writes are themselves table calls, so the body must be async), `remove`, `delete`, `restore` and the three bulk verbs through the cheaper sync-body `wrapExclusive`.
