| <a id="fjs-619"></a>FJS-619 | litestone — **a field `@allow('read')` that reads only the caller was evaluated once per field per ROW through the expression interpreter** | 2026-08-31 | The 2026-07-18 audit's **M7**, the worst per-row cost on its list, and the one place a read policy is answered in JS rather than in SQL — `FJS-D129` compiles a field read predicate into the WHERE so a caller cannot FILTER by a column they may not read, but which columns come back on a returned row is still a per-row strip. `@allow('read', auth().isAdmin)` has ONE answer for a whole result set and was asked once per field per row. **The classifier is an ALLOW-LIST and that is the whole of its safety**: `referencesRow` names the node kinds that read only the caller — `literal`, `auth`, `and`, `or`, `not`, `compare`, `ternary`, `list` — and anything else, including a kind the language grows later, is assumed to read the row and evaluated per row. | <a id="fjs-603"></a>FJS-603 | litestone — **`@@unique` took no predicate, so *one OPEN row per parent* — the constraint effective dating is built on — could not be declared, and the near miss was refused with the opposite answer** | 2026-08-31 | **`@@unique([cols], where: <expr>)`**, and it does not reopen `FJS-204`: that ruling refused a predicate the FRAMEWORK derives onto every unique index, and this is one the AUTHOR declares over a domain column. | <a id="fjs-593"></a>FJS-593 | litestone — **An enum member had to be a legal identifier, so a closed set written for a person to read could not be expressed at all** | 2026-08-29 | `enum S { Draft }` parsed and `enum S { "On Hold" }` did not. Each landed as a bare `String` with the constraint gone. **A member may be a quoted string now, and the stored value IS the string** — no second name, nothing translates. That is Postgres's own answer. Prisma's `@map` on the member is the other one and buys a separate code-name at the price of a bidirectional layer on every read and write, which nothing in the corpus asks for; `@label` already covers display, so the code-name would be a third thing. | <a id="fjs-591"></a>FJS-591 | litestone — **An index column could not carry a direction, so a composite index whose columns disagree was inexpressible — and the migrator could not have seen one anyway** | 2026-08-29 | `@@index([a, b])` took a bare field list. trigger.dev writes `@@index([organizationId, type, createdAt(sort: Desc)])` twenty-one times; every one imported as an ascending index, which serves a different set of queries. **Adopted Prisma's spelling, and it is ZenStack's too**: `stdlib.zmodel` in both v2 and v3 declares `@@index(_ fields: FieldReference[], …, sort: SortOrder?, …) @@@prisma` — byte-identical, and `@@@prisma` is their own marker for *inherited unchanged* — so one spelling covers all three and an import carries it through. `Asc`/`Desc`, and lowercase is accepted because it is the client's own `orderBy` word for the same thing. **`fields` stays a plain array of names** and the directions travel beside it as `sorts`, aligned by position, because the index NAME is derived from the field list and three other readers walk it. **Three places in the migrator were blind to it and all three had to move.** `indexKey` did not carry the direction, so a declared `sort: Desc` compared equal to the ascending index already there; the added-index emit rebuilt its column list from names alone, so the drop would have been followed by a CREATE of the index it had just removed; and `parseIndexColumns` de-quoted `"createdAt" DESC` into `createdAt" DESC`, which `isIndexExpression` then reported as an expression — the [`FJS-584`](#fjs-584) shape one modifier along. | <a id="fjs-583"></a>FJS-583 | litestone — **A scaled column promised an exact round trip and stopped delivering one at 2^53, silently — the exact failure `@scale` exists to prevent** | 2026-08-29 | `docs/exact-numbers.md` said nine places leaves "nine figures in front of the point", reasoning from SQLite's 64-bit `INTEGER`. But the value crosses a JS `number` at both ends and litestone sets `safeIntegers` nowhere, so `bun:sqlite` returns a `number` on every path — a column read and an aggregate alike. Measured: `12345678900000001` reads back `…000`, `9007199254740993` reads back `…992`, `sum()` rounds the same way. At nine places the true range is **seven** figures, not nine, and two distinct minor-unit values collide into one row value with nothing raised. | <a id="fjs-575"></a>FJS-575 | litestone — **`@scale` caps at 9 places and usage-based billing writes 15 — but the cap was never the binding constraint, and raising it would have made things worse** | 2026-08-29 | The row asked for a bigger cap. A bigger cap would have moved that hole further into the dark. **What the corpus actually needs splits in two**, and Lago's own `Fee` writes both: `amountCents Int` beside `preciseAmountCents numeric(40,15)`, `unitAmountCents Int` beside `preciseUnitAmount numeric(30,15)` — and `preciseCouponsAmountCents` at scale 5, which `@scale` took cleanly. A **rate** is small-magnitude and many-placed, and `@scale(9)` holds every rate in the 25 columns found across lago, discourse and triggerdev. A **precise accumulated total** is big-magnitude *and* many-placed, fits no 64-bit integer at any useful scale, and is an un-rounded intermediate rather than a stored quantity — so where it lives is rounding and allocation, which is [`FJS-D154`](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d154), since ruled. Prior art agrees on the split: Postgres has `NUMERIC` and we do not; **Stripe writes two fields** — an integer `unit_amount` beside `unit_amount_decimal`, *"a decimal string with at most 12 decimal places"* — and Prisma's `Decimal` on SQLite is broken by its own maintainers' account (`prisma#20635`), which is why `Int @scale` exists at all. | <a id="fjs-573"></a>FJS-573 | cli — **A crashed deploy stranded its lock, and the pid recorded in it was the pid of a shell that had already exited — so nothing could tell a stale lock from a live one, and the resume the journal was offering could only be reached by deleting a file by hand** | 2026-08-29 | Ruled rather than patched ([FJS-D156](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d156)): the journal owns *what state did the last run leave*, the lock owns *is another run working here*, and the lock only ever looked like a second answer to the first because it could not expire. A better pid was not available and never could be — `fli` runs on the operator's machine and reaches the target one command at a time, so **there is no process on the target to point at**. So the lock records what is true: the run, who started it, when, and **which step it is inside** — the fact that makes the duration beside it mean something, since four minutes in `04-build-api` is a build and four minutes in `06-swap` is a run that died. The step comes from a `beforeStep` announcement in the step runner, which is the only place it can: the build is the longest thing a deploy does and runs BEFORE the journal opens (`04c-journal`), and a timer cannot serve it because `execSync` blocks the loop for the whole of a step. Neither register judges liveness — that is a fact about a process this machine cannot see — so the refusal reports and names both ways out: **`fli deploy --resume`** continues what the journal holds and takes the lock over, **`fli deploy:unlock`** drops it and starts fresh. A resume was always safe without a probe (a succeeded step replays into a no-op, a step is claimed compare-and-set, and different bytes are a different Release and therefore a new transition); the lock was only what made it unreachable. A TTL was considered and refused — the heartbeat can only tick per step, so the TTL would have to exceed the longest build. One format, one parser, four scripts, three readers (`core/lock.js`) where each of `deploy`, `deploy:status` and `deploy:doctor` used to `cat` the file and read it its own way — `deploy:status` split `<pid>:<iso>:<target>` on `:` and had been reading the hour as the timestamp for its whole life. | <a id="fjs-569"></a>FJS-569 | litestone · junction — **`busy_timeout` was set on four SQLite connections and absent from four others — and the number was a literal an app could not change** | 2026-08-29 | **`busy_timeout` is set on four SQLite connections and missing from four others, so which databases wait under contention is an accident of which file opened them.** Measured 2026-08-29 with two connections, one holding the write lock: with `busy_timeout = 5000` the second waits 5007ms; **with no pragmas at all it fails in 1ms**. Two things fell out: `MESSAGE_KEYWORDS` had claimed `time: ['format']` for as long as the emitter produced no format, so an author’s `@time(message:)` was keyed to a keyword no consumer could ever check; and the seconds variant was two alternative regexes where one optional group says the same thing — the flag WIDENS what may be stored and does not make a finer value mandatory. **Still nothing in this repo declares one**: `example` and `basecamp` hold 141 `DateTime` columns and zero `@time`, `@date` or `@datetime`, so this is covered by unit tests on both sides of the wire and by no drive. 19 cases in `test/time-column.test.ts`, 3 in sierra’s `form-fields`; litestone 3136 pass, sierra 1144 pass. The framework's headline guarantee is that you never invalidate, because the server says what changed; on a detail screen that guarantee is simply false, and it is false in the silent-wrong-data class — the page renders, the numbers are stale, nothing throws. **Two rows of one model can also disagree with each other**: the store is per-`resource()` call (`const store = new Store<T>()` inside `resource()`), so two `createResource('orders')` in two route files are two copies, kept in step only because both subscribe to the same service. Unbound it is what it always was, which is what the fifteen `Store` cases in `client.test.ts` are the negative control for. Lifetime is a **TTL** (`nodeTtlMs`, default 30s) rather than a reference count the application maintains, which is the part of Apollo and Relay everyone complains about. `resource.record(id)` is the view of one; Sierra's wraps it so the first read goes through the resource's own `_call('get')` — its hooks, its coercion, its `@version` — while Junction keeps the rule about WHEN to read. **A push moves the value and does not move the remembered version**, which is `FJS-341` restated as a test: the node is the synced truth and the view is what this screen READ. `example`'s order detail is the first caller and its two manual `await load()` after an action are gone — that reload was the app hiding this. **Proven in a browser**: `verify:live` gained a third question (17 assertions, up from 14) — a watcher tab on the detail page, the order paid from node over HTTP on a session of its own, the status moving with `sameDocument: true`. Negative-controlled: reverted to `service.get(id)` it reads `{"status":"pending","moved":false}`. | <a id="fjs-525"></a>FJS-525 | caravan — **a fixed-time schedule fired zero times in spring and twice in autumn** | 2026-08-25 | The firing path asked *does the current minute match*, which on the two days a year when the local clock is not a function of real time gave two wrong answers. Measured through the real path — `renderComponent` over `<p>{text}</p>` with `text = '<img src=x onerror=alert(1)>'` emitted `<p><img src=x onerror=alert(1)></p>` — and at the bare serializer, where `div.textContent = '<script>alert(1)<\/script>'` reads back as live markup. No manifest key, no language change, no parser — a line scan over a file in `node_modules`, reached through that package's own `exports` map. **Fixed 2026-08-24** as `fli check`'s twenty-seventh rule, `package-model-drift`. A WARNING and not an error, because a deviation can be right and the reader has to judge: both declarations are printed, and `check-baseline.json` is how an app accepts one it has argued for. **Its first run on basecamp found three things and closed all three, one of them in the package rather than the app.** (1) `User.emailVerified` and (2) `User.role` had lost `@allow('write', auth().isAdmin)` — basecamp gates update at USER(4) with `@@allow('update', id == auth().id)`, *your own row*, so the field policy is the only thing between a caller and their own `emailVerified`, and marking your own address verified is skipping the verification. **Latent rather than live**: basecamp exposes no `users` service and its gate grades on `status` and `WorkspaceMember.role`, neither of which is this — it becomes real the day a profile screen writes through a service over `db.user`. Both restored, and both now appear in `db/access.snapshot.md`, so a future removal is a diff. (3) `User.accountId` was `String?` against auth's `Int?` — and here the PACKAGE was wrong: every id `@frontierjs/auth` declares is a uuid, so an `Int?` could not hold one, which is what made the column unusable for the one app that reached for it. auth ships `String?` now; `SessionContext.accountId` was always a string either way. Seven cases in `test/checks.test.js`, mutation-checked both directions — never comparing, and comparing the APP's columns instead of the package's (the false-positive shape), each turn it red. Green: cli 848, auth 244, basecamp 143 + 301/301 · [checks.js](packages/cli/core/checks.js) · [checks.test.js](packages/cli/test/checks.test.js) · [user.lite](packages/auth/db/user.lite) · [schema.lite](packages/basecamp/db/schema.lite) |

Equal is allowed — an admin appointing an admin is what the role is for. The hook is registered per method rather than on `all`: `role` is a word two other models use, and a hook grading every payload carrying the key would refuse a fleet write for holding the wrong kind of role. **6 tests in `api/test/services.test.ts`, mutation-checked** — neuter the hook and two go red, the self-check one, the outrank check one. The test must PARSE the emitted output, not merely assert a clean compile; asserting the compile is what let this run. Filed S3 rather than S2 because the trigger requires the author to pick one of nine specific names; the cost once triggered is S2-shaped — silent at compile, loud and misdirected at runtime · **Fixed 2026-08-23.** `BUILTIN_LOCALS` names the thirteen injected names beside `RESERVED_WORDS`, and `analyzeScript` walks its own `ast.body` — not `vars`, which carries neither function nor class declarations, both of which collided — refusing every declaration form by name. It THROWS rather than pushing to `errors`, because the call site downgrades that whole array to warnings and a module that does not parse is not a warning. Scoped to the factory, so a nested `const $props` is still legal; over-refusing there would break code that never collided. Verified 65/65 refusals across five declaration forms including destructuring, with eight controls still compiling and parsing. Seven cases added to `test/emission.test.js`. Green: mesa 1233 vitest + 82 runtime-browser + 47 vite-browser, `@frontierjs/ui` 857 with 69/69 components opened. The surface was found to be 13 names rather than the 9 first measured — `$inspect` collides only when `debug !== false`, and `$ctxProvide`/`$ctxRead` only where `$context` is in use, which is why the reserved set is keyed off what the compiler MAY inject rather than what a given config does inject · [compiler.js](packages/mesa/src/compiler.js) · [emission.test.js](packages/mesa/test/emission.test.js) · [FJS-D132](DECISIONS.md#fjs-d132) · [VISION.md RULE 18](packages/mesa/docs/VISION.md) |

| <a id="fjs-366"></a>FJS-366 | junction — **Every WebSocket connection was evicted after 30s, in every app, because the keepalive had a server half and no client half** | 2026-08-20 | The channels plugin evicted any connection that had not sent `{type:'ping'}` in 30s, sweeping every 10s. `JunctionClient.startHeartbeat()` sends that ping and **nothing called it** — not junction, not sierra, not `fli new`'s scaffold — so a fresh app opened a socket, received `{type:'connected'}`, and was closed with `connection evicted` ~35s later, forever. Reported from a scaffolded app; measured there as a 39.4s close and a reconnect ~1s after each. Invisible unless watched, because the socket carried no event and the reconnect succeeded: a live list simply never updated. Two things were wrong under it. **Only a ping refreshed liveness**, so a client in the middle of service calls over that same socket was evicted while plainly alive. And **the client's default interval was 30s against a 30s timeout**, so calling it would have raced the reaper anyway. Fixed by moving the drive to the SERVER — it pings an idle socket every 15s and evicts one silent for 40s, and any frame counts as liveness, malformed ones included. The client answers from its message handler rather than a timer, which is what keeps a backgrounded tab connected: browsers throttle timers to ~1/min in a hidden tab, slower than any eviction window, and a message handler is not throttled. `channels(setup, { heartbeatInterval, heartbeatTimeout })` are the knobs; `startHeartbeat()` stays for a client whose server predates this, now defaulting to 15s. `test/heartbeat.test.ts` runs the loop against a real socket at 100ms/400ms — idle is pinged, silent is evicted, pongs hold it, ordinary traffic holds it, and the shipped client holds it with no call by the app |

| <a id="fjs-351"></a>FJS-351 | litestone — **A generated validation case did not isolate the rule it named, in both directions** | 2026-08-19 | `generateValidationCases` built every case from ONE attribute with no idea what else sat on the field. **A boundary claimed a value the field refused** — `@length(3, 200)` on an `@email` column produced `'xxx'`, so the write was refused and the runner reported *@length allows this value and the write was refused*. Measured on a six-field schema: 8 of 12 boundary cases false, 4 of 6 fields reported broken when nothing was, and the fix a reader reaches for is deleting a rule from the schema. **An invalid case was refused by somebody else's rule and counted as proof of its own** — `''` on that column is rejected by `@email`, so the two cases naming `@length` proved nothing about it. Measured by disabling `@length` in `validate.js`: on a single-rule field the runner says *the schema declares @length(3,20) and the write was ACCEPTED*, on the `@email` field it said **nothing**, and the only entries there were the two false alarms — which appear whether the rule is enforced or not, so the checker could not tell an enforced `@length` from a missing one, and the false alarm is what hid it. The same measurement now yields four findings, all naming `@length`, and zero on a schema with nothing wrong with it. `attempt()` also carried the message every case declared and never compared it; it does now, as a backstop for an implementation refusing for a reason the schema did not predict. Both closed against one judge: `validateField` is now exported from `core/validate.js` — the function that decides this on a real write — because a table of formats in the generator would be a second definition of every rule. **It is asked about the field's OTHER rules only**: whether a value satisfies or breaks the rule it NAMES is established by construction, and asking the implementation makes the runner its own oracle — the first version did, and disabling `@length` then reported *not checked* instead of *the write was ACCEPTED*, losing the finding the runner exists to produce. Caught by measuring rather than by reasoning. **The repair is format-blind**: it grows or trims the factory's own valid sample and asks the validators, so an email grows in front of its own domain and `@startsWith("ORD-")` keeps its prefix with no code here containing either word; shrinking works on alphanumeric RUNS and leaves punctuation alone, which turns `email1@example.com` into `e@e.c` at five. Which dimension is free depends on the rule — a boundary IS its length, an invalid `@length` case need only sit outside the bound, every other rule's length is incidental. What cannot be isolated is `uncheckable`: named, with the blocking rules' own messages, because a rule that stops being asked about is this runner's failure mode one layer up — and **`litestone mutate` excludes it from the kill count**, since a row generated from the original schema appears identically under every mutant, which is the shape the 22 `error` rows had when they scored a 14-mutant schema 93%. Five tests, and basecamp's `Invitation.email` carries `@email @length(6, 200)` again — 6 rather than 5 because `a@b.c` is the shortest string `@email` accepts, so a bound at the floor is unviolatable and the runner says so |

| <a id="fjs-349"></a>FJS-349 | basecamp · conduit · junction — **The three endpoints an Outpost calls took no credential at all, and one of them redirected the fleet** | 2026-08-19 | Measured before and after, against a running API. | <a id="fjs-294"></a>FJS-294 | caravan — **Two Caravan instances on one `jobs.db` each fire every cron and each reset the other's in-flight jobs** | 2026-08-18 | The second of the two candidate answers: coordinate for real, rather than declare single ownership and refuse a second opener — a refusal would also refuse the ordinary shapes, a web process that only dispatches beside a worker that only runs, and it would state an assumption the deployment gets to make. **A running row is OWNED.** Each instance takes an id, stamps it on every row `claimNext` takes, and heartbeats into a `job_owners` table on a timer; recovery reclaims only rows whose owner has gone quiet past `lease` (30s, `heartbeat` 5s, both settable from `junction.config.js`). `markDone`/`markFailed` are guarded on the owner as well as on `running`, so a reclaimed job's late completion cannot land on the attempt that replaced it, and a clean `stop()` drops the owner row — but only with nothing in flight, since past `pool.stop()`'s deadline a handler may still be running and dropping it then invites exactly the double execution the owner prevents. **The cron half is the dedup key, not leader election**: the fire is dispatched under `cron:<job>:<epoch-minute>`, so every instance fires its own schedule and all but the first are the no-op a stated id already is (`FJS-D35`). The fix is not to thread the three missing filters through: it is that a second SELECT path exists at all. Either the recursive step carries the same policy SQL and the whole path runs through the plugin runner like every other read, or `recursive` becomes a where-shape the normal query pipeline compiles. | <a id="fjs-008d"></a>FJS-008d | vscode — **Completion offers attributes instead of types on any line that already has one.** | 2026-08-06 | **Fixed 2026-08-06.** `atTrigger` was `trimmed.includes('@')` over the WHOLE line, ignoring the caret, so editing the type in `status OrderStatus @default(pending)` — the shape of most real field lines — offered `@id`/`@unique` and never `OrderStatus`. Now read off `line.slice(0, character)`: `attrToken` (`/(@@?)(\w*)$/`) means "typing an attribute name", `inArgsOf` (`/@@?(\w+)\([^)]*$/`) means "inside that attribute's arguments". The five branches that keyed off `line.includes('@@gate')` and friends switched to `inArgsOf` — `@relation` had to, since it rode on `atTrigger` and the caret is past the `(` by then — and the type list is now suppressed inside an argument list, where a gate level is not a field type. 7 new caret assertions, incl. two caret columns on ONE line giving two different answers [server.ts:238](packages/frontierjs-vscode/src/litestone/server.ts#L238) |

| FJS-006 | `@encrypted` on a `Json` field silently destroyed the value | 2026-08-06 | `encryptField` does `String(plaintext)`, so an object became `'[object Object]'` and what got stored was a faithful ciphertext of that literal — unrecoverable, nothing thrown. A Json field is now serialized before encryption and parsed after decryption, mirroring the pipeline either side (write encrypts then serializes; read parses then decrypts), keyed on the DECLARED type captured in `buildFieldPolicyMap`. Objects, nested structures, arrays and JSON scalars all round-trip; the column stays ciphertext and no plaintext reaches the file. `@secret`, `$rotateKey` and `searchable` verified too. 9 tests, 4 fail if reverted. The `CLAUDE.md` hazard telling people to use `String @encrypted` instead is removed |
| FJS-005 | `$setAuth(user).sql` was byte-identical to unscoped `sql` — raw SQL bypassed every access rule | 2026-08-06 | Raw SQL is now available through `asSystem()` only, on any schema declaring `@@gate`/`@@allow`/`@guarded`/`@encrypted`/`@scoped`. Measured before: `$setAuth({id:1})` gave 1 row via the ORM and 3 via `.sql`, with a `@guarded` column in plaintext — and the UNSCOPED client was wider still (ORM 0 rows vs `.sql` 3), which is why the rule covers `db.sql` too and overturns the idea file's "unchanged". Coarse per schema rather than per statement on purpose: a hand-written SQL validator that is subtly wrong grants a false guarantee, and `bun:sqlite` exposes no authorizer (verified). Three byte-identical copies of `sql` collapsed to one runner. 9 tests, 5 fail if reverted. Ruled in `DECISIONS.md` § Access control. **Scoped raw SQL (the view set in `IDEAS/scoped-sql.md`) is deliberately NOT built** — revisit with `herald` |
| FJS-004 | A model service had no way to say "read only" — an admin could forge a row into an append-only audit trail | 2026-08-06 | `methods: ['find','get']` \| `'readOnly'`, enforced in `callService` so an in-process caller is refused exactly as the wire is. CRUD and actions share the list; unknown names throw at construction; `/manifest`, `/metrics` and OpenAPI filter by the same predicate. 21 tests, 7 fail if the check is removed. Basecamp's `/audit` dropped four hand-written stubs for one line and was re-probed live: `405 {"message":"Service 'audit' does not offer 'create' (allowed: find, get)"}`. Ruled as [FJS-D07](#fjs-d07) |
| FJS-002 | `cookieAuth: true` could not authenticate a request | 2026-08-06 | Junction's `extractToken()` read only `authorization: Bearer` and `x-api-key`, so the cookie the auth plugin set was never read back and the documented mode gave you a session you could not use. `extractToken` now takes an optional cookie name and @frontierjs/auth calls `app.http.setAuthCookie('session')` from its own `register()`, so cookie mode is ONE switch — requiring the app to also write `config.auth.cookie` would have left a half-configured state reproducing the original bug. Cookies stay **off by default** as a CSRF decision (a Bearer token cannot be forged cross-site, a cookie travels automatically; `SameSite=Lax` is what makes it safe when on), and an explicit credential always beats the ambient one. Covers the WebSocket upgrade too — otherwise a cookie-authed app connected its socket anonymously, silently. Marker test flipped from 401 to 200; 12 junction tests + 5 auth tests, 7 fail if reverted |

| FJS-068 | mesa — **`renderComponent` resolved bare imports from Mesa's own package root (SSR_SPEC W1)** | 2026-08-03 | `renderComponent` / `renderFile` take `options.tmpDir`, threaded through the recursive `compileTree` path so an import graph cannot be split across two directories, and the directory is created if missing. The renderer compiles each module to a temp `.mjs` and imports it, and Node resolves a bare specifier relative to the *importing* file — so where those temp modules live decides which `node_modules` a rendered tree can reach; it was a module-level `const` resolved at import time, making the directory a property of the package rather than of the call. **The default deliberately stays Mesa's own package root**, because a temp module carries `import '@frontierjs/mesa/runtime.js'` and that has to resolve from wherever it is written; pointing them at the app's tree is the caller's statement, and `sierra/src/build/index.js` makes it (`node_modules/.sierra/render`), which is what makes a prerendered layout containing `import { page } from '@frontierjs/sierra/router'` render at all. Four cases in `render-component.test.js` including the negative one — the same import must still fail under the default, or the test proves nothing. **Closed in code 2026-08-03; the row and three doc lines said "open" until 2026-08-16**, which is the only thing that was wrong with it since |
